fields.title: The False Sense of Security
fields.deployment_context:
The Rivertown City Council wanted to make its city planning more modern in 2019. They hired a cutting-edge Geospatial Decision Support System to speed up the approval process for a new housing complex beside the river.

The system's main goal was simple: to replace slow, manual surveying with an AI that could quickly sort land parcels. It would put land into one of two groups: Zone A (Safe for Construction) or Zone B (High Risk).

The system's result was hard to argue with because it was based on high-resolution LiDAR (laser elevation) scans and 50 years of rainfall data. A clear, bright blue line on a 4K interactive dashboard separated the river from the land. Everything behind the border was a calm, flat green colour and said "0% Risk."

The High-Def Map with the clear "Safe" line
fields.intended_use:
In 2021, a "1-in-100-year" storm hit the area, breaking the illusion of safety. The amount of rain was 15% more than the highest amounts ever recorded that were utilised to train the model.

The algorithm quickly turned out to be wrong. The river surged higher than expected, and the model thought the local flood walls were perfect, but they started to leak. The water went over the digital "blue line" and into the "Green Zone."

Those who were affected: 500 homes in the new estate were flooded. Most of these people, 90%, didn't have flood insurance. They thought they were safe because the dashboard said they were in the "Official Safe Zone." An audit did not find the failure. People in the "Safe Zone" only noticed it during the crisis, when they said water was getting into their homes.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Dangerous Assumptions

The AI formed two wrong assumptions that weren't true. Stationarity: It thought that climate trends in the future will be similar to those in the last 50 years. It didn't take into consideration climate change, which causes bad weather to happen more often. Infrastructure Reliability: It worked on the idea that the concrete flood walls would never break, even when cracks or maintenance problems could happen.

2. The 'False Precision' Design Decision

The user interface was the biggest problem. Instead of a fuzzy gradient, the developers elected to show a sharp, binary line (Safe vs. Unsafe). This was a deliberate design choice to make the tool look "cleaner" and more official for lawmakers who aren't very tech-savvy. This made False Precision, a high-resolution image that hides data that isn't very reliable.

3. Problems with Governance and Organisation

There was no "Human-in-the-Loop." To speed up the permitting procedure, the system's output was taken as the whole truth. No hydrologist was given the job of manually checking the "edge cases" near the flood wall, which meant that the AI's blind spots went unchecked.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Environmental AI needs to be able to show uncertainty. We should never use harsh lines to show risk. Instead, interfaces should employ colour gradients (fading from green to red) or clear probability percentages (such as "80% Safe") to show consumers when the model isn't sure.

Warning for Users: Don't believe "High Resolution." Even if a map looks accurate (has a lot of pixels) and official, that doesn't ensure the prediction it makes is right. A pretty map can nonetheless be based on maths that isn't comprehensive.
fields.description: How the 'High-Definition' Flood Map of Rivertown Let Down 500 Families

fields.title: The Misread Landscape
fields.deployment_context:
In 2020, the Southern European Forestry Commission put in place a system that uses satellites to predict the risk of wildfires. The AI looked at the density of plants, the moisture in the soil, the wind patterns, and past burn data to make daily danger maps for regional fire services.

The system was created and tested in the temperate woods of Northern France and Germany, where it was able to accurately anticipate fire outbreaks 48 hours in advance with a 94% accuracy rate. Its creators promoted it as a "universal" instrument for fighting wildfires, and agencies in southern Europe were keen to use it before their summers become even more perilous.

The dashboard made maps that were neat and colour-coded: green for low danger, amber for moderate risk, and red for high risk. Every morning, fire service commanders used these maps to set up teams and equipment ahead of time.
fields.intended_use:
A terrible wildfire broke out in July 2022 in a coastal scrubland area of southern Portugal.

In 36 hours, the fire burnt about 12,000 hectares. Three communities were evacuated, and 14 individuals went to the hospital because they breathed in smoke.

The AI had given the region a "Low Risk" (green) rating on the morning of the fire. Firefighters had to move 80 km north to a forested slope that the model said was "High Risk." That hillside never caught fire.

Detection: A volunteer fire guard called in the alarm. The fire had already crossed two roads by the time the personnel were sent to a different location. The analysis after the disaster showed that the model had been inaccurate all summer along the whole coast.

Part 3: Why It Didn't Work (Analysis)

Training Data Mismatch (Domain Shift)

The model was mostly trained on deciduous and coniferous forests, which are tall, wet-canopy areas where the density of the canopy and the moisture in the soil affect how fires behave. Mediterranean scrubland is very different. Even when satellite images show little vegetation, low, dry, oily bushes like cistus and rosemary burn quickly and intensely.

The AI thought that "low vegetation density" meant "low fuel load." In reality, it meant "ground fuel that burns quickly and is very flammable."

2. Seasonal Assumptions

The model gave a lot of weight to recent rainfall as a protective factor. Summer rain is prevalent in temperate climates. Months can go by in the Mediterranean without rain, and the model's idea that "recent rainfall reduces risk" was fundamentally wrong for the region's dry summers.

3. No Local Calibration or Feedback Loop

The system was put in place without adjusting its thresholds to fit the local conditions. Fire commanders have no way to mark faulty forecasts and send corrections back into the program. The map that was made each morning was seen as the truth.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: It is necessary to evaluate any environmental prediction system against local historical data and recalibrate it for local vegetation, climate, and topography before using it to predict a new area. This step is known as "domain adaptation," and skipping it could be deadly.

Warning for Users: A high accuracy score from training does not mean the model will perform well in your region. Always ask: "Where was this trained, and how similar is that environment to mine?" If the vendor cannot answer clearly, treat the outputs with extreme caution.
fields.description: How a Wildfire Prediction Model Trained on Temperate Forests Failed in the Mediterranean

fields.title: The Seasonal Blind Spot
fields.deployment_context:
In New Zealand, a national conservation organization used drone video to set up a computer vision system to keep an eye on protected wetlands. The AI learned how to recognise plant species in aerial photos and mark alien species that could harm native ecosystems.

The training dataset had more than 200,000 annotated photos that were mostly taken between October and February, which is spring and summer in New Zealand. In these months, native and invasive species seem very different. For example, natural flax has wide green leaves, while invasive willow has catkins and lighter leaves.

During preliminary testing in the summer, the system was able to accurately identify 91% of species. Ecologists praised it as a major step forward for large-scale monitoring.
fields.intended_use:
During its first autumn and winter cycle (March to August), the system's accuracy fell to 58%. More importantly, the false negative rate for invasive willow rose to 73%, which means that almost three out of four invasive plants were being called native. 

The result was very poor as AI-generated reports that indicated invasive species were "under control" kept a 400-hectare wetland restoration project going for four months. When ecologists came to check on the work in person once a year, they saw that willow had spread over 30% of the area that was being restored. It was thought that the cost of the cleanup would be $2.1 million NZD. 

Detection: The failure was only found on a regular annual field visit, neither by the AI or by anybody else watching its outputs.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Seasonal Bias in Training Data

Most of the training shots were from spring and summer. During specific times of year, species have different visual traits, like the form and colour of their flowers and leaves. A lot of plants shed their leaves, change colour, or seem the same in the autumn and winter. The AI had never seen what invasive willow looks like when it is not growing.

2. No Concept of Temporal Change

The model saw each picture as its own snapshot. It didn't have a way to keep track of how a piece of land changed over time, which would have shown how invasive species spread. A quick check of "this area is getting greener in winter when it shouldn't be" would have found the problem.

3. Over-Trust in Automated Reports

The conservation agency stopped sending people to the field every month and started sending AI reports every week instead, thinking the technology was better. But no one was regularly looking at the AI's confidence levels, which decreased a lot throughout the winter but were averaged into summary numbers that hid the drop.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Training datasets must encompass the complete spectrum of variables that the model will face, including seasonal fluctuations, meteorological factors, and exceptional scenarios. This means that before saying a model is "ready for deployment," you need to collect data from all seasons for environmental monitoring.

Warning for Users: An AI that works great in the summer could not work at all in the winter. Always ask yourself: does the training data cover the conditions I'm using it in? If the model has only seen the globe in one season, it can't see anything for six months.
fields.description: How a Biodiversity Monitoring AI Misclassified Invasive Species as Native Due to Training Gaps

fields.title: The Uneven Eye
fields.deployment_context:
A health tech business released a mobile app in 2019 that let users take pictures of moles or skin blemishes that looked suspicious and get an instant risk assessment. The app's AI was a deep convolutional neural network that had been trained on more than 150,000 clinical photos from dermatology databases in the US and Western Europe.

In clinical studies, the app was as good as or better than general practitioners in finding melanoma, with a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 89%. It was sold as a way to make dermatological screenings more accessible to everyone, especially in places where it takes a long time to get an appointment with a specialist.

In its first year, the app was downloaded more than 2 million times and got a lot of positive press as an example of "AI for good."
fields.intended_use:
A dermatological research team at a university hospital in Lagos, Nigeria, did an independent test of the app in 2021. They used a set of 3,000 clinical photographs from patients with Fitzpatrick skin types IV–VI (medium brown to dark brown skin). The findings were really bad.

The app missed two out of three melanomas because it was only 34% sensitive for detecting melanoma on darker skin. It was even worse because the app gave false reassurance to 61% of verified malignant lesions on dark skin, calling them "Low Risk."

The researchers found at least 12 examples where patients used the app, got a "Low Risk" rating, and then put off going to the doctor. Three of these individuals came back months later with melanoma that had gotten worse.

Detection: An outside academic research found the failure, not the firm or its own monitoring.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Homogeneous Training Data

Less than 5% of the 150,000 training photos showed skin types IV–VI. The model had mostly trained to find melanoma on light skin, where the difference in colour between healthy skin and malignancies is greater. The visual signs of melanoma are less obvious on darker skin and seem different. The AI didn't have many examples to learn from.

2. Evaluation Bias

The first clinical trials took place at hospitals in the US and UK, where the majority of patients had lighter skin tones. The 95% sensitivity that was reported was correct, but only for the group that was tested. Prior to the debut, there was no examination of subgroups based on skin type.

3. Absence of Demographic Safeguards

The software didn't ask users what sort of skin they had, and it didn't notify them that performance would be different. There was no way to mark circumstances where the model's confidence was low because the input characteristics were new to it. The model's performance on each user's skin tone didn't matter; everyone got the same clean % score.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Before they can be used, medical AI systems must be tested on a wide spectrum of patients. It is necessary for every clinical examination to include subgroup analysis based on age, sex, ethnicity, and skin type. "Average accuracy" can disguise dangerous differences.

Warning for Users: An AI that works well "on average" might not work well for you. Be careful with the results of a health app if it doesn't say who it was tested on. A reassuring result from a tool that hasn't been well tested can be worse than no result at all because it might make you wait longer to get real medical help.
fields.description: How a Skin Cancer Detection App Performed Dangerously on Darker Skin Tones

fields.title: The Dangerous Reassurance
fields.deployment_context:
In 2021, a regional health authority in the UK tried out an AI-powered triage chatbot to cope with the growing number of calls to its 111 non-emergency helpline. The chatbot asked patients a set of structured questions about their symptoms and then put them into one of four triage categories: self-care advice, GP appointment, urgent treatment, or call 999.

The chatbot learned from anonymised records of more than 500,000 prior 111 calls. It used both decision-tree logic and a natural language processing model to understand free-text reports of symptoms. When tested against past call outcomes, the chatbot agreed with human call handlers 87% of the time.

The health authority thought that the chatbot would cut down on call wait times by 40% and let human operators focus on the most difficult situations.
fields.intended_use:
A clinical safety study found 23 incidents where the chatbot told patients with heart problems to "monitor at home and contact your GP within 48 hours" after being in use for more than six months. Eight of these patients went to A&E within 24 hours with confirmed acute cardiac events.

The common pattern: patients aged 30–45 who reported chest tightness, shortness of breath, and fatigue, but did not report the "classic" symptoms the chatbot weighted most heavily, such as crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm. The chatbot's risk model put a lot of weight on age as a protective factor. Younger people always got a lower risk score for heart issues.

In two instances, patients indicated that the chatbot's reassurance actively postponed their decision to phone 999. One patient had to wait an extra nine hours before their partner made them go to the hospital.

Detection: The issue was found after a regular clinical audit every six months, not by the chatbot's real-time monitoring systems.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Over-Weighting Age as a Protective Factor

The training data showed a real statistical pattern: elderly patients are more likely to have heart problems. But the model learnt this connection too well, taking age as almost a given instead of just one among several factors. A 35-year-old person who had classic heart problems was nevertheless rated as "low risk" since their age alone made the chance of escalation too low.

2. Anchoring on 'Classic' Symptom Descriptions

The chatbot's NLP model learned from old descriptions that were more dramatic and textbook-like, such "crushing pain" and "pain in left arm." Patients who used less technical language to describe their symptoms, such "tight chest," "can't catch my breath," or "just feel wrong," got lower urgency scores. The model punished unclear language instead of seeing it as a possible sign of an unusual presentation.

3. No Escalation for Uncertainty

When the chatbot wasn't sure (less than 60% confidence), it went with the lower-risk group instead of sending the question to a human operator. This was a planned design choice to keep the human queue from getting "overwhelmed," but it meant that instances that were not clear-cut, which are the ones that need human judgement, were always under-triaged.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: In triage systems that are crucial to safety, ambiguity should lead to escalation, not de-escalation. If the AI isn't sure, a human must be involved by default, even if that makes things less efficient. A longer phone queue is nothing compared to a missed heart attack.

Warning for Users: If an AI chatbot tells you your symptoms aren't serious, but you know they are, trust your gut and go to the doctor nevertheless. AI triage tools are not diagnosis; they are screening techniques. They cannot substitute for clinical judgement, particularly in cases of atypical symptom presentations.
fields.description: How an AI Triage Chatbot Told Chest Pain Patients to 'Wait and Monitor'

fields.title: The Efficiency Trap
fields.deployment_context:
In 2019, a large NHS hospital trust implemented a predictive algorithm to optimise bed allocation across its three hospitals. The system analysed patient data and diagnosis codes, length of stay history, readmission rates, and recent A&E attendance to predict which incoming patients would need beds and for how long.

The goal was to reduce bed shortages during winter surges by predicting demand 72 hours in advance and pre-allocating capacity. The algorithm was trained on three years of hospital admission data and initially reduced bed shortages by 18% in its first quarter.

Hospital managers praised the system for finally bringing "data-driven decision-making" to a process that had historically relied on ward managers' intuition and whiteboard planning.
fields.intended_use:
After 18 months, a junior doctor noticed a troubling pattern: patients with complex chronic conditions, particularly those with multiple long-term illnesses managed in the community were consistently being assigned to the lowest bed-priority tier. Some were waiting 12+ hours in A&E. Corridors for beds the algorithm had allocated to patients with acute but less complex needs.

An internal review found that the algorithm had learned an unintended pattern. Chronically ill patients who were well-managed by community care teams had fewer recent hospital admissions. The model interpreted "few recent admissions" as "low need," when in reality these patients had low admissions precisely because of good ongoing care and when they did present at hospital, it was typically because something had gone seriously wrong.

The review identified 47 cases over six months where chronically ill patients experienced delayed bed allocation, contributing to longer A&E waits and poorer outcomes, and in three cases, escalation to intensive care that clinical staff believed could have been avoided with earlier ward admission.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Proxy Variable Trap

The algorithm used "recent admission frequency" as a proxy for clinical need. For most patients, this is a reasonable heuristic. But for well-managed chronic patients, low admission frequency signals effective care, not low severity. The model couldn't distinguish between "healthy and rarely needs hospital" and "seriously ill but well-managed outside hospital."

2. Outcome vs. Process Confusion

The training data captured outcomes (admissions, length of stay) but not the clinical reasoning behind them. It didn't know why a patient was or wasn't admitted, only whether they were. This meant it optimised for historical patterns without understanding the clinical context that produced them.

3. No Clinical Override Mechanism

Ward managers and A&E, consultants could see the algorithm's priority scores but had no formal mechanism to override them without escalating to hospital management. In practice, this meant clinicians deferred to the algorithm even when their own judgment disagreed, because challenging the system was bureaucratically slower than waiting for a bed.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Algorithms that use historical patterns as proxies for need must be tested for perverse incentives. Ask: "Could a good outcome in the past make the model think this patient needs less help in the future?" If yes, the proxy is dangerous and needs clinical safeguards.

Warning for Users: Data-driven allocation is not the same as fair allocation. An algorithm that optimises for efficiency may systematically disadvantage the patients who most need protection. Clinicians must always retain the ability and the authority to override automated prioritisation.
fields.description: How a Hospital Bed Algorithm Deprioritised the Patients Who Needed Care Most

fields.title: The Loop That Couldn't Stop
fields.deployment_context:
In 2017, a metropolitan police force in the American Midwest adopted a predictive policing platform. The system ingested ten years of arrest records, 911 call logs, and incident reports to generate daily "crime probability heatmaps" colour-coded maps showing where crime was most likely to occur in the next 24 hours.

Officers were dispatched to patrol the highest-probability zones. The police chief praised the system publicly, saying it would "put officers where they're needed before crime happens, not after." In its first year, arrests in targeted zones increased by 32%, which the department cited as proof the system was working.

The dashboard was slick and intuitive: red zones meant "deploy more officers," yellow meant "monitor," green meant "low priority." Each morning, patrol commanders received a fresh map and allocated their shifts accordingly.
fields.intended_use:
By 2019, civil liberties organisations and community groups raised alarms. An independent analysis by a university research team found that the same six neighbourhoods which were all predominantly low-income, majority-Black communities had been flagged as "high risk" every single day for over two years.

The data told a clear story of a feedback loop. More officers were sent to these neighbourhoods.

More officers meant more stops, more searches, and more arrests including for minor offences (possession of small amounts of cannabis, jaywalking, loitering) that went largely unpoliced in wealthier, predominantly white areas. These new arrests were fed back into the system as "evidence" of high crime, which reinforced the heatmap's prediction, which sent more officers, which generated more arrests.

Meanwhile, areas with known but under-reported crime (domestic violence in suburban areas, white-collar fraud in the financial district) remained perpetually green on the map. The model didn't predicted policing instead of crime itself.

Detection: The feedback loop was identified by an external academic study commissioned by a civil liberties group, not by the police department's own oversight processes.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Historical Bias Baked Into Training Data

The ten years of arrest data reflected a decade of existing policing priorities and racial disparities. Areas that were historically over-policed had disproportionately high arrest records which not necessarily because more crime occurred there, but rather because more policing occurred there. The model learned to replicate these patterns as if they were objective truths about where crime happens.

2. The Feedback Loop (Runaway Effect)

Predictive policing creates a closed loop where predictions drive deployment, deployment drives arrests, arrests drive predictions. Without external data to break the cycle such as victimisation surveys, hospital admissions, or anonymous reporting, the system has no way to distinguish between "high crime area" and "heavily policed area." The two become indistinguishable in the data.

3. No Equity Audit or Disparity Monitoring

The system had no mechanism to monitor whether its predictions disproportionately affected specific racial or socioeconomic groups. There was no threshold that would trigger a review if the same neighbourhood was flagged as high-risk for, say, 30 consecutive days. The absence of an equity audit meant the disparity grew silently for over two years before anyone with authority noticed.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Any predictive system whose outputs influence the data it is later trained on is vulnerable to feedback loops. These loops can amplify existing biases exponentially. The only defence is external validation data that the system cannot influence and mandatory equity audits that flag demographic disparities before they become entrenched.

Warning for Users: An increase in arrests is not the same as a decrease in crime. If a predictive system is evaluated by the volume of enforcement actions it generates, it will optimise for enforcement, not safety. Always ask yourself "Are we measuring outcomes for communities, or outputs of the system?"
fields.description: How a Predictive Policing Heatmap Created a Self-Fulfilling Prophecy of Over-Policing

fields.title: The Postcode Penalty
fields.deployment_context:
A county court system in the southern United States started using a recidivism risk assessment tool in 2018 to help judges make choices about bail and punishment. The system employed a logistic regression model that had been trained on five years of court records. It gave each defendant a score from 1 (low risk) to 10 (high risk).

Age, previous convictions, employment situation, education level, history of substance misuse, and, most importantly, home postcode were all part of the input features. The developers said that the postcode was a stand-in for "community stability," which studies showed was linked to rates of reoffending.

The judges were warned that the tool was simply for advice and that they should use their own judgement. In reality, a review by the county's public defence office later revealed that judges accepted the algorithm's advice in 84% of cases.

2: The Pattern No One Questioned

A journalist got the scoring data in 2020 by making a freedom-of-information request and then wrote an article about it. The results were clear: defendants from five specific postcodes, all of which were low-income and mostly Black, had risk scores that were an average of 2.7 points higher than those of defendants with the same criminal records residing in wealthier, mostly white locations.

The research brought to light the case of Marcus, a 24-year-old first-time offender who was found guilty of stealing something that wasn't violent. He had a steady career, no history of drug or alcohol misuse, and close family ties. His risk score was 7 out of 10, which means he was "high risk." A white defendant with a very similar profile but a suburban postcode received 3, which means he was "low risk." Marcus was given a prison sentence. The other defendant got a community order.

The journalist looked over 15,000 instances and concluded that the postcode was the best predictor of a high score, even more so than having a criminal record or being unemployed. The instrument was punishing people for being poor and living in bad neighbourhoods.

Detection: Investigative journalism, not the judicial system or the tool's developers, found the difference.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Postcode as a Proxy for Race and Poverty

In a country with deep residential segregation, postcode is strongly correlated with race and socioeconomic status. Including it as an input feature meant the model was, in effect, using race and poverty as predictors of reoffending, even though race was not an explicit input. This is known as "proxy discrimination": the model achieves a discriminatory outcome through a correlated variable that appears neutral on the surface.

2. Correlation Mistaken for Causation

People from disadvantaged postcodes do statistically reoffend at higher rates. But this is driven by systemic factors such as lack of employment opportunities, inadequate housing, reduced access to rehabilitation services, not by individual character or intent. The model treated a societal failure as an individual risk factor, punishing defendants for the conditions they were born into.

3. The 'Advisory Only' Illusion

Even though it was called "advisory," the tool's number score had a strong anchoring effect. Judges, especially those with a lot of cases to handle, used the score as a way to think more quickly. The 84% compliance rate reveals that "advisory" really meant "decisive." The way a statistic was framed as clean, clear, and computer-generated gave it more authority than narrative-based assessments did.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Any aspect that has a strong correlation with a protected characteristic (such as race, gender, religion, or handicap) should be examined as a possible sign of discrimination. Common proxies include name, school attended, language spoken, and postcode. If there are still proxies, taking the protected attribute out of the input doesn't make the model fair.

Warning for Users: A risk score is not a fact about a person. It is a hypothesis based on patterns in past data. The score will also show structural disparity if the data does. Before using a score to decide someone's future, judges, employers, and other decision-makers need to know what it means, how it was made, and what it can't tell them.
fields.description: How a Recidivism Scoring Tool Branded Low-Risk Individuals as High-Risk Based on Where They Lived

fields.title: The Digital Red Line
fields.deployment_context:
A mid-sized bank in the UK started using an automated lending platform to handle personal loan applications in 2019. The method used a gradient-boosted decision tree model that had been trained on eight years of payback history for 1.2 million historical loans.

The input features were the applicant's credit score, income, length of work, debt-to-income ratio, current credit utilisation, and the postcode of their home. The bank's data science team used postal code as a sign of "local economic stability," saying that the state of the economy in a region affected the chances of getting paid back.

The automated system accepted loans 60% faster than human underwriters in A/B testing, while the default rate was only slightly lower: 3.1% compared to 3.4%. The bank thought it would save £8 million a year by lowering its processing costs.
fields.intended_use:
A charity that helps people with their rights checked things out in 2021 utilising paired test applications. Fake applicants with the same salary, credit score, job history, and debt levels were sent from different postcodes. The findings were really bad.

People from postcodes in mostly ethnic minority neighbourhoods in East London, Birmingham, and Bradford were turned down for jobs at almost twice the rate of people from wealthy, mostly white suburbs with the same qualifications. When loans were authorised, people from disadvantaged postcodes were offered interest rates that were, on average, 1.8 percentage points higher.

The organization said that the algorithm had turned down about 4,200 creditworthy candidates from low-income areas over the course of two years. These applicants would have been approved under the traditional method, which involved people reviewing applications. Most of these people came from Black, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi groups.

Detection: A consumer rights nonprofit found the discrimination through paired testing, not through the bank's own compliance systems.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Postcode as a Proxy for Ethnicity

In the UK, historical immigration, housing policy, and socioeconomic disparity have a big impact on where people live. There is a strong link between postcode and ethnicity. The model learned that living in a minority-majority location meant a higher probability of default, even when the financial characteristics of the people were the same. The model automated a pattern that would be prohibited if it were done by hand.

2. Historical Data Reflects Historical Inequality

The eight years of repayment data includes the time after the 2008 financial crisis, when unemployment and default rates were much higher in poor areas than in other areas. The program learned these patterns as permanent parts of particular postcodes, not as short-term effects of an economic shock. It developed a permanent awareness of who is creditworthy by baking in a crisis.

3. Compliance Testing Looked at the Wrong Things

The bank's compliance team checked the model to make sure it didn't include any protected traits like ethnicity, gender, or religion as inputs. But they didn't check to see if similarly qualified applicants from various groups got the same treatment. This is the most important difference between "fairness of inputs" and "fairness of outcomes." The bank only assessed the first one.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Financial models need to be checked for different effects on protected groups, not just for the absence of protected characteristics in the input. One of the best ways to find automatic discrimination is to use paired testing, which means sending in the same profiles from separate groups.

Warning for Users: Digital redlining is harder to detect than a red line on a map, but it has the same effect: people in some areas can't get jobs or other opportunities because of where they live, not who they are. You can ask for an explanation if you are turned down for a loan. If the answer doesn't make sense based on your financial situation, the system might be the issue, not you.
fields.description: How an Automated Loan System Recreated 1930s-Style Redlining Through Postcode Data

fields.title: The Joke That Crashed the Market
fields.failure_type: NLP-Driven Sentiment Analysis / High-Frequency Trading Bot
fields.deployment_context:
A quantitative hedge firm used an NLP-powered trading bot in 2022 to scan news feeds, social media, and financial wire services in real time. The bot employed sentiment analysis to find breaking news that could change stock values and made trades in less than a second, which is much faster than any human trader could do.

The system learned from five years of headlines about financial events and how the market moved after them. It had learned to connect certain words with price changes: words like "bankruptcy," "fraud," and "collapse" made people sell, while words like "acquisition," "record profits," and "expansion" made people buy.

The bot made 23% more than the benchmark in backtesting. The fund told investors that it was proof that "machines read markets better than humans."
fields.intended_use:
"BREAKING: MegaCorp Industries Announces Bankruptcy After CEO Loses Entire Treasury in Crypto Poker Tournament" was the headline of a popular satirical finance blog in March 2023. It was evident that the article was a joke because it had silly details regarding a made-up "Blockchain Texas Hold'em" league.

The trading bot didn't get the joke. It read the headline, pulled out "MegaCorp Industries," "bankruptcy," and "entire treasury," and then, in less than 400 milliseconds, it put a huge short bet on MegaCorp stock. The fund had a lot of money, so the sell pressure set off algorithmic stop-losses at other funds, which caused a chain reaction.

In just 90 seconds, the price of MegaCorp's stock fell by 8.2%. By the time human traders and compliance officers figured out what had happened—a funny article—the damage had already spread. Three other funds had made automatic trades based on how the price moved, and regular investors who had put stop-loss orders had their positions sold at the bottom of the drop.

The market bounced back in 12 minutes, but not before an estimated $340 million in value was lost. Because their stop-loss orders went through at the crash price, many ordinary investors lost money for good.

Detection: Human traders at other companies found the funny article and reported it as strange. From the bot's point of view, it had done the right thing by responding to bad news. Its own monitoring systems didn't find anything strange.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. No Understanding of Context or Tone

The NLP model used keywords to figure out how people felt about something. It could tell that "bankruptcy" is bad, but it couldn't tell the difference between a real news story, a funny article, an opinion piece, and a made-up situation. It didn't know what source credibility, genre, or tone meant. Every text was treated as if it were true.

2. Speed Prioritised Over Verification

The technology was meant to make trades within milliseconds of seeing a signal. This speed was what made it stand out from the competition, but it didn't give anyone time to check. There was no point in the pipeline where it was reviewed to see if the source was a reliable news source, if other news sources were covering the same subject, or if the information was marked as satire or opinion.

3. Cascade Risk Was Unmodelled

The bot was set up to get the best returns for itself. The people who built it didn't model or test what would happen if its transactions were big enough to impact the market and set off other algorithms. In a market where many bots react to price changes made by other bots, one wrong trade might set off a chain reaction that affects the whole system.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Helpful Tips: Source verification and genre classification are two things that NLP systems employed in high-stakes, time-sensitive situations must have. You shouldn't treat a headline from a satirical blog the same as a headline from Reuters. At the very least, computers should keep a list of reputable sources and either flag or throw away stuff from sources that aren't recognised or are meant to be funny before taking any action.

Warning for Users: Being fast doesn't mean you're smart. A system that can react in milliseconds but can't discern a joke from a fact is not smart; it's too fast and too unsophisticated. In the financial markets, acting on faulty information can cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
fields.description: How a Trading Algorithm Misread a Satirical News Headline and Triggered a Flash Crash

fields.title: The Crossing It Couldn't See
fields.deployment_context:
Delivery to the last mile without a driver

In 2022, a logistics company started a test run for self-driving delivery drones on the ground in a medium-sized city in England. The drones employed a mix of LiDAR, GPS, and camera-based computer vision to find their way around sidewalks, cross streets at approved crossings, and deliver packages to homes.

The computer vision system had learned to find traffic signals, pedestrian crossings, curbs, obstructions, and moving pedestrians by looking at more than 2 million annotated photographs. During 14 months of testing in dry weather, the drones made 98.6% of their deliveries without any problems. People commended them for cutting down on delivery van traffic in residential areas.

Based on these results, the pilot was expanded from 3 to 12 communities.
fields.intended_use:
A delivery drone flew over a busy residential street in November 2023, when it was raining heavily. The white stripes on the crossing were hard to see because of standing water and illumination from car headlights. The drone's computer vision system thought the crossing was a "standard road surface marking," which means it was a lane divider, not a pedestrian crossing.

The drone didn't stop because it was misclassified. It got onto the road at the same time that a 72-year-old woman walked across from the opposite side. The drone hit her ankle at a slow speed (around 6 mph), which made her tumble. She broke her wrist and had a lot of bruises.

A nearby store's security cameras caught the event. It showed the drone going right into the crossing without stopping, even though the pedestrian had the right of way.

Detection: The pedestrian, spectators, and CCTV all saw the failure. The drone's internal logs showed that it had correctly classified the crossing on the way out (when it was dry), but incorrectly classified it on the way back (when it was wet).
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Weather-Dependent Perception Failure

Most of the data used for training was obtained while it was dry or cloudy. Fewer than 8% of the training photographs showed wet surfaces with standing water or glare that reflected light. The model had learnt to distinguish zebra crossings by their high-contrast white stripes, but when it rained, the contrast was greatly diminished by the glare and reflection of the water, which made the pattern less clear.

2. No Redundant Safety Classification

The drone used just one computer vision model to find crossings. There was no backup method, such a map-based search for recognised crossing points or a LiDAR-based identification of elevated curb patterns, to use when the primary model wasn't very sure.

3. Confidence Threshold Set Too Low

The algorithm thought the wet crossing was a "lane marking" with 54% confidence, which is just over chance. A person looking at that confidence score would see that it was very uncertain. But the system's threshold for acting on a categorisation was set at 50%. This meant that a result that was almost a coin flip was enough to move on without stopping. There was no "I'm not sure, slow down and wait" attitude.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Autonomous systems that work in public places need to be taught and tested in all kinds of weather, such as rain, snow, fog, glare, darkness, and ice. Also, safety-critical perception judgements should never be based on only one model. When one sensor type fails, redundant systems (such as map data, LiDAR, and radar) provide important backup.

Warning for Users: A method that works 98.6% of the time when the weather is nice can not work at all when it's terrible. The reported reliability numbers for an autonomous system are wrong if it hasn't been tested a lot in the settings it will actually work in. The last 1.4% could include situations where someone gets hurt.
fields.description: How an Autonomous Delivery Drone Mistook a Pedestrian Crossing for a Road Marking in Heavy Rain

fields.title: The Intersection Freeze
fields.failure_type: Autonomous Shuttle / HD Map Navigation System
fields.deployment_context:
In 2021, a university in the Netherlands used two self-driving electric shuttles to take students and staff from its research park campus to the city center train station. The shuttles travelled a 3.5 km route over dedicated lanes and highways with little traffic.

The shuttles employed pre-mapped routes in high definition (HD) along with LiDAR and camera data in real time. The HD graphic showed the exact positions of lanes, traffic lights, crossing spots, and expected road markings down to the centimetre. The system compared what its sensors saw to what the map suggested should be there.

The shuttles carried 45,000 people in six months of operation and were praised as a model for environmentally friendly city transit. The service was available from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., and at busy times, a shuttle left every 15 minutes.
fields.intended_use:
As part of an update to the cycling lane, the city council painted over the road markings at a busy crossroads along the shuttle route in March 2022. The revised markings pushed the stop line 1.5 meters forward and put a box for bikes to go first in front of the vehicle stop line.

The first shuttle came at the crossroads the next morning and stopped, but not at the new stop queue. Its HD map stated the stop line was 1.5 meters behind it, and its cameras could see the new painted line in front of it. The two inputs didn't agree with each other.

The shuttle's dispute resolution mechanism couldn't figure out which input to believe. It went into a safety hold, with the engine running, the doors locked, and it not moving. It stayed at the junction for 22 minutes before someone on the other end of the queue was called, detected the problem, and manually overrode the shuttle to let it go.

The identical freeze happened seven more times at the same intersection over the next three days. During busy times, shuttles that were stuck in the lane caused traffic jams. The institution stopped the service for two weeks to update the map.

Detection: People on the shuttle told us right away that the freeze had happened. The remote operations team found the root cause within hours.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Brittle Map Dependency

The system was set up to rely on its HD map as the main source of information about how the roads are laid out. The map got out of current right away when things in the real world changed, as when the markings were repainted. It wasn't easy for the system to deal with a discrepancy between its map and its sensors because it was built to assume that the map was always right.

2. No 'World Has Changed' Reasoning

The shuttle could tell that the road markings didn't match the map, but it couldn't figure out why. A person driving would quickly comprehend, "Oh, they've moved the stop line forward and added a bike box. I'll stop at the new line." The shuttle's logic was simple: either there was a match or there wasn't. It didn't know how roads change, how to build or fix things, or that the fresh visual evidence should take precedence over the older map.

3. No Communication Between City and Shuttle Operator

The city council painted the road again without telling the shuttle driver. There was no set way for letting autonomous vehicle operators know about changes to the road, and the operator didn't have a way to get or use those updates. Both groups thought the other would take care of it.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Autonomous systems that use pre-built maps need strong ways to find, mark, and adjust to changes in the real world. This includes being able to think about why things don't match up ("the map might be out of date"), safe fallback behaviours (such moving slowly instead of stopping), and ways to quickly update the map.

Warning for Users: The physical world is always changing. For example, roads are painted over, signs are relocated, and barriers are put up. Any autonomous system that relies on a static map of a world that changes will ultimately run into a problem. The question is not if it will happen, but how the system will deal with it when it does.
fields.description: How a Self-Driving Shuttle Froze at a Junction Because Road Markings Contradicted Its Map

fields.title: The Combination It Never Saw
fields.deployment_context:
A chemical processing factory in Germany put in an AI-powered safety monitoring system in 2020. The system took in data from more than 300 sensors, such as temperature probes, pressure gauges, flow meters, gas detectors, and vibration sensors. It then utilised a deep neural network to find unusual patterns that may mean equipment failure, leaks, or unsafe circumstances.

The algorithm learned from four years of sensor data, which included 14 documented accidents that safety engineers had manually classified. It was made to work with, not replace, the plant's human safety officials. When the AI found something wrong, it sent an alert to a central dashboard for them to see.

In its first 18 months, the system correctly identified three real problems with the equipment: a broken pump bearing, an unusual temperature gradient in a reactor vessel, and a steady loss in pressure in a storage tank. All of these problems were found before human operators did. People started to trust the system more.
fields.intended_use:
A valve seal in a chlorine handling unit started to break down progressively over the course of several weeks in August 2022. The degradation caused a mix of sensor readings that were all within normal operating limits on their own. For example, one pipe's temperature went up a little, the flow rate in the line next to it went up a little, and the gas concentration reading went up but not high enough to set off an alarm.

There was no alarm from just one sensor. The AI's anomaly detection model, which was taught to find patterns of abnormality, said with 78% confidence that the overall system condition was "normal." The 22% uncertainty was recorded, but it didn't lead to an increase.

On Tuesday morning, the seal entirely disintegrated. A leak of about 15 kg of chlorine gas happened 40 minutes before a human operator on a routine tour smelt the gas and shut down the system. There were twelve workers who had to leave, three of them had to be treated for chlorine exposure, and the plant part was closed for six weeks.

Detection: A person walking across the area found the leak by smell. The AI system didn't notice anything strange before, during, or after the leak started.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. The 'Novel Combination' Problem

Every sensor reading was within the typical range. The risk was in the combination: a certain pattern of small differences across several sensors that, when taken together, showed that the seal was getting worse. But this same combination had never happened in the four years of training data. The model couldn't tell what it was because it had never seen it before. It was trained to find patterns of known anomalies, not to figure out new ones.

2. Threshold-Based Individual Sensors

The gas detector said that the chlorine levels were high, but they were still below the warning level that was hard-coded. The AI saw each sensor's threshold as a binary gate: if the value was over the threshold, it was a possible abnormality; if it was below the threshold, it was normal. It didn't take into account how sensors can interact with each other or whether having several sensors close to their top limits at the same time might be a hint of trouble.

3. Confidence Score Ignored

The system only had 78% confidence that the state was "normal," which is lower than the 95%+ confidence it usually has for truly normal conditions. This decline in trust was noted, but nothing was done about it. When the system's confidence was low, there was no policy for what to do. There was no notice to a safety officer, no request for a manual inspection, and no flag on the dashboard.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Anomaly detection systems need to be able to see not only patterns that are already known, but also when things aren't typical. If numerous sensors are close to their individual limits at the same time, even if none of them goes beyond their limit, the combined condition may be strange. You need to keep an eye on confidence scores and do something about it. If confidence drops, you should look into it, not just write it down.

Warning for Users: AI safety systems are strong at spotting trends they have seen before. They are not good at finding new ways that things may go wrong, which are the most dangerous ones. Never assume that the AI is observing everything and stop doing physical safety checks, routine walkthroughs, and using your own judgement. The failures that are most hazardous are the ones that the system wasn't trained to see.
fields.description: How an Industrial Safety AI Missed a Chemical Leak Because Its Sensor Fusion Model Had Never Encountered That Combination of Readings

fields.title: The Regulation That Didn't Exist
fields.deployment_context:
In early 2023, a borough council in outer London put an AI chatbot on its website to help people with questions about council services. It was based on a big language model with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. This means that it was expected to get responses from the council's own planning documents, bylaws, and guidance pages before making a response.

The council advertised the chatbot as a way to cut down on wait times at the call center, which had been as long as 40 minutes during busy times. People might raise questions regarding trash collection, council tax, noise complaints, and, most importantly, planning rules for home and business improvements.

When compared against a set of pre-approved answers, the chatbot got 89% of the questions right in initial tests. The council went forward with a public launch.
fields.intended_use:
Priya, who owned a small business, asked the chatbot in June 2023 if she needed planning approval to turn the ground floor of her building from a store into a cafe. The chatbot replied with confidence, "Under the General Permitted Development Order (Class E), changing a property from retail to cafe use doesn't need planning permission as long as the property is less than 150 square meters and has been used for retail for at least two years."

Priya's property met both of these requirements. She followed this advise and hired a contractor to start renovations, spending about £28,000 on plumbing, kitchen extraction, and interior fit-out. Six weeks later, a council enforcement officer came to see her and told her that the conversion did need planning permission because of local rules that put further limits on her conservation area.

The chatbot's answer was mostly true regarding the national rule but utterly wrong about the local exception. There was no mention of the "150 square metres" threshold or the "two years" condition in any municipal document. The chatbot had made up detailed, believable details that weren't real.

Priya was told to stop working and file a retrospective planning application. She lost £9,000 in rent and contractor standby costs because of the delay. Her application was finally granted, but only after changes that made it more expensive.

Finding the mistake: A council enforcement officer found the mistake during a normal check, not the chatbot or its operators.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Hallucination: Confident Fabrication

Big language models make writing that is statistically likely to be true, but not always true. When the RAG pipeline couldn't get a detailed answer from council papers because the issue was about both national and local rules, the model made up plausible-sounding facts to fill in the gaps. The model made up the "150 square metres" barrier and "two years" requirement since they seemed like something that would be in a planning rule.

2. RAG Pipeline Retrieval Failure

The council's library had national planning guidance and local bylaws in distinct documents that were set up in different ways. The RAG system got national guidelines (which was only partly useful), but it didn't get the local conservation area rules (which were very important). The retrieval stage identified something that made sense, and the model thought that was enough. It didn't have a way to know that the retrieval was incomplete.

3. No Disclaimer or Confidence Indicator

The chatbot always spoke in a confident, authoritative way, whether it had found a reliable source or made up the material itself. There was no disclaimer noting "this answer has not been checked against local laws," no confidence score for the user to see, and no suggestion to check the advise with a planning officer before acting on it.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Public authorities that use AI chatbots must make it clear that their answers are not legal or regulatory advice. When there is no source, the chatbot should mention such instead than making up a reasonable answer. For important questions like planning, legal rights, and benefits, the chatbot should tell consumers to talk to a real person.

Warning for Users: A chatbot that sounds sure of itself is not the same as one that is right. Language models are made to write language that seems fluent and authoritative, even if they are making stuff up. Never make a financial decision based only on what a chatbot says. Always check with a real person first.
fields.description: How a Council Chatbot Hallucinated a Planning Rule, Costing a Business Owner Thousands

fields.title: The Story That Never Happened
fields.deployment_context:
In 2022, a digital news aggregator included an AI-powered "daily briefing" option. Every morning, customers got a customised summary of the day's top stories, which were shortened from several sources into short, easy-to-read paragraphs. The technology employed a big language model to put together articles from all over the web into clear summaries.

A lot of people liked the service. After six months, 1.4 million people were reading the AI-generated briefings as their main source of morning news. "Every story, every angle, in one paragraph" was a big part of the company's marketing.

During the first month, the editorial crew did random checks on the summaries. The checks were cut down to once a week and then once a month after the system consistently made correct summaries during this time.
fields.intended_use:
On the same day in February 2023, two different news stories broke. A chemical facility in eastern Germany said there was a little ammonia leak. No one was hurt, and the leak was closed within two hours. In a another news story, a hospital in western Germany said that its A&E department will be closed for a short time since there weren't enough staff members.

The AI summariser looked at both events and came up with this report: "A chemical plant explosion in Germany has forced a nearby hospital to close for an emergency, and officials are warning that patients may be exposed to ammonia." Emergency services are there.

This summary was completely wrong. There was no blast. It was 400 kilometres away and had nothing to do with the hospital closing. Ammonia did not hurt any patients. But the AI combined two stories that each featured the phrases "Germany," "emergency," "closure," and "hospital" into one more dramatic story.

About 340,000 people viewed the fake summary before it was reported. People shared it on social media, where it was screenshotted and reproduced without the original source's context. A German news outlet in the area spent three hours proving the story wrong. The stock price of the chemical company fell 2.3% in the morning before going back up.

A user who had read both original articles independently noted that the summary didn't match either one and used the app's feedback option to report it.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Cross-Contamination in Multi-Source Synthesis

The model was made to combine information from several articles into one summary. The model's attention mechanism thought two unconnected stories were related when they used the same surface-level keywords, therefore it combined their information. It didn't understand things like distance, time, or the cause-and-effect links between occurrences; it merely understood how often phrases happened to be used together.

2. Narrative Coherence Bias

Language models are designed to generate text that is easy to read and makes sense. A dramatic story ("explosion forces hospital closure") is easier to read and understand than two separate, boring pieces ("minor leak contained" and "A&E closed for staffing"). The model's optimisation for fluency actively encouraged it to combine the stories, since the combined version was a better story, even though it wasn't real.

3. Reduced Editorial Oversight

The first round of meticulous spot-checking found no mistakes because the system worked effectively on routine summaries. But the editorial checks got less and less as more people used the system, which meant that it was least overseen when it had the most users. The mistake happened during a time when checks were done every month. It may have gone unnoticed for weeks before an editor saw it.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: When AI summarisation systems combine information from several sources, they need to be able to do two things: entity resolution (is this the same event?) and source separation (are these tales really related?). Summaries should have links to the original sources so that users can check the assertions. Before publishing, there should be automated fact-checking, such making sure that locations, dates, and entities are the same across all combined sources.

Warning for Users: A summary made by an AI is not a report; it's a reconstruction. It might mix, simplify, or make up connections between real occurrences. If a summary sounds dramatic or shocking, look at the original sources. Be very careful with the summary if there are no sources that are linked to it.
fields.description: How an AI News Summariser Merged Two Separate Events Into a False Narrative

fields.title: The Papers That Didn't Exist
fields.deployment_context:
In 2023, an environmental consulting firm started employing a big language model to write parts of Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) for clients that wanted to build on land. The AI would write background literature studies, describe ecological hazards, and make initial suggestions, which would save analysts about 60% of the time it takes to write.

The way the consulting firm worked was: AI made a draft, a senior analyst looked it over and made changes, and then the client and the local planning authority got the final product. The AI was told to back up its statements with academic citations, using its training data to find papers that were relevant.

The method worked at first. Customers were happy with how quickly the reports were sent, and the first three reports passed planning authority inspection without any problems.
fields.intended_use:
In March 2024, an officer from the planning authority who was looking over an EIA for a proposed housing construction near a wetland Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) decided to investigate the report's references. The report used 34 scholarly publications to back up its findings about how biodiversity affects the water table and how habitats connect.

The officer looked for the first five citations. Three were not real. The authors were real professors, the journals were real journals, and the years of publication were reasonable, but the papers with those titles and findings had never been published before. Two of the three fake citations backed up the report's most important claim: that the proposed development would have "negligible impact on the adjacent wetland ecosystem."

A complete examination of the report determined that 11 of the 34 citations (32%) were made up. The other 23 were authentic, but in some cases, the AI had correctly credited a study but wrongly or selectively summarised its conclusions.

The application for planning was put on hold. The consulting firm had to send in a new report that was written entirely by people. The developer thought it would take six months longer and cost an extra £180,000.

The consultancy received a formal complaint from its professional organization.

Detection: A hard-working planning official who verified citations by hand. The consulting firm's own review process hadn't found the lies.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Citation Hallucination

Large language models don't get citations from a database; they make them up. The algorithm generated author names, journal titles, and paper titles that were statistically reasonable according to its training data, yet did not correspond to any actual publication. This is citation hallucination: the model makes a reference that looks authentic because it knows how to format and style academic citations, not because it has checked if the reference is real.

2. Misrepresentation of Real Papers

Even when the model used an actual paper, it sometimes talked about things that weren't in the paper. The algorithm made an educated guess about what the document "probably" said based on the topic and what it knew in general, not what it actually said. This is less obvious and harder to find than plain lying, because the paper is real and related to the issue.

3. Review Process Trusted the Format

The senior analyst who looked over the AI draft reviewed the story for consistency and the suggestions for logic. They didn't check each citation because it would have taken too long to check 34 of them, and since the citations appeared right. The arrangement was great, with real author names, authentic journals, and dates that made sense. This gave the impression that the information was reliable.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: There must be an obligatory verification step in any workflow that employs AI to make citations. This stage checks each reference against a real database, such as Google Scholar, DOI lookup, or a library catalogue. You shouldn't believe a language model's citation until you know it exists. This verification must be written down and able to be checked for important documents like EIAs.

Warning for Users: AI-generated citations are the most harmful type of delusion because they appear just like real citations. It's almost impossible to find a fake reference that has a real author's name and a real journal title without checking. Always check the references when you are looking at a document that was made with AI. This is where the model is most likely to make things up.
fields.description: How an AI-Generated Environmental Impact Report Cited Non-Existent Academic Studies

fields.title: The Invisible Penalty
fields.deployment_context:
In 2020, a UK institution that only accepts a small number of students used a machine learning model to help sort through the growing number of applications from undergraduates. The approach gave applicants a score from 0 to 100 based on their expected grades, the keywords in their personal statement, and their extracurricular activities. Academic reviewers looked at applications that scored higher than 70. Applications that scored lower than 50 were automatically rejected. Applications that scored between 50 and 70 were put in a secondary review pool.

Five years' worth of data on successful applicants were used to train the extracurricular part. The model figured out which activities were linked to getting into college and doing well in school after that. Things like "Model United Nations," "Duke of Edinburgh Gold Award," "debating society president," and "orchestra" did very well.

The university thought that standardising the first round of screening would help decrease unconscious prejudice. The admissions director said it was "fairer than a tired professor reading their 200th personal statement at midnight."
fields.intended_use:
An internal equity evaluation looked at the admission rates of different types of schools in 2022. The results were very clear: applicants from independent (private) schools were 2.4 times more likely to pass the automated screening stage than applicants from state schools with the same qualifications, even after taking anticipated grades into account.

The extracurricular scoring part was to blame. Model UN, rowing, polo, international exchanges, and CCF (Combined Cadet Force) are all activities that private school applicants do a lot of. These activities showed up a lot in the training data and got high marks. Part-time job, caring for others, volunteering for local groups, and coaching younger students are all things that state school applicants do a lot of. These activities were less common among successful applicants in the past and got low or no ratings.

The model had learned that "Duke of Edinburgh" was important while "part-time job at Tesco" was not. It didn't get that both show commitment, time management, and resilience; it simply knew which one showed up more often in the profiles of kids who had already been accepted, most of whom came from private institutions.

The assessment found that some 320 state school applicants had been immediately rejected or put lower on the list during two admissions cycles when they should have been given a complete academic review.

Detection: The university's own internal equality investigation found the difference after the widening participation office expressed concerns.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Historical Bias in Training Data

The model learned from five years of successful applicants to a selective university that has always had a lot of private school students. The training data used the extracurricular profiles of wealthy pupils as a model for success. There were too many activities that needed money, family connections, or schools with a lot of extracurricular activities. There weren't enough activities that students from low-income families could take part in.

2. Proxy for Socioeconomic Status

Extracurricular activities serve as an indicator of familial affluence and educational resources. You need an instrument and lessons to play in an orchestra. You need money and a school that offers exchanges to do "international exchange." "Cared for younger siblings while parents worked" doesn't demand anything, yet it shows real responsibility and maturity. The model thought the first two were important but not the third.

3. No Contextual Understanding

The model couldn't grasp that getting A*AA grades while working 15 hours a week at a supermarket is probably more amazing than getting the same marks without a job and a lot of help from tutors. It gave scores to acts without taking into account the situation in which they were done.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: It is important to evaluate admissions algorithms to see if they have different effects on different socioeconomic groups, school kinds, and demographics. When rating extracurricular activities, you need to think about the chance, not only the sort of activity. To make sure the model looks at accomplishment in relation to opportunity, it should include contextual admissions data such school performance, eligibility for free school meals, and community deprivation.

Warning for Users: An algorithm that has learned from past accomplishments will choose people who look like those triumphs. The algorithm will keep giving advantages to people who have had a lot of success in the past, even though it looks like it is being fair. "Data-driven" does not mean "fair."
fields.description: How a University Admissions Tool Penalised State School Applicants by Misvaluing Their Extracurriculars

fields.title: The Filter That Learned to Discriminate
fields.deployment_context:
A big IT company used an AI-powered CV screening tool in 2019 to handle a huge number of applications, over 50,000 per three months. The system used natural language processing to read CVs and give candidates a score from 1 to 5 depending on how well they were likely to do in technical roles.

The model was trained on ten years of hiring data: CVs of applicants who had been hired and subsequently rated as "high performers" by their managers. The logic was to learn what successful employees' CVs look like then find more people like them.

In its first six months, the tool reduced recruiter screening time by 75% and was described internally as "the most impactful HR technology investment in five years."
fields.intended_use:
In 2021, an internal diversity audit revealed that the proportion of women advancing past the CV screening stage had dropped from 34% (under human screening) to 19% (under AI screening).

The drop was consistent across all technical role categories.

An investigation by the data science team found two primary patterns driving the disparity. First, the model had learned to penalise career gaps of 6 months or longer. In the training data, career gaps correlated with lower performance ratings, but this correlation was driven by managers who rated returning employees lower in their first review period, not by genuine long-term performance differences. Since women are disproportionately likely to take career breaks (maternity leave, caregiving), the career gap penalty was effectively a gender penalty.

Second, the model penalised CVs that mentioned women's sports leagues ("women's football captain," "netball team"), women's professional networks ("Women in Tech member"), and women's colleges. These terms appeared rarely in the training data (which was 78% male) and the model learned to associate them with lower-probability candidates. The word "women's" had become a negative signal.

The audit estimated that over two years, approximately 1,200 qualified women had been automatically downranked below the recruiter review threshold.

Detection: An internal diversity audit, prompted by declining representation metrics noticed by the HR analytics team.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Career Gap Penalty as Gender Proxy

Career gaps correlated with lower first-review performance ratings in the training data. But the causal mechanism was not that career gaps reduce capability, it was that managers tended to rate returning employees conservatively. The model couldn't distinguish between "this person is less capable" and "this person's manager scored them lower for reasons unrelated to ability." This resulted in a stand-in for parental leave became a stand-in for gender.

2. Gendered Language as Negative Signal

The model saw every phrase in a CV as a possible predictor. In a training dataset that was 78% male, any term strongly associated with women appeared disproportionately in the minority group. "Women's football" was mostly on women's resumes. The model learns that this phrase is a bad sign because it shows up on CVs that are less likely to fit the prevalent pattern (male). The model didn't get gender; it got how often words were used.

3. Performance Rating Bias in Training Labels

The training labels "high performer" vs. "not high performer" and were based on manager ratings, which themselves contained gender bias. Research consistently shows that women receive lower performance ratings than men for equivalent work, particularly in male-dominated fields. Training a model on these ratings means training it to replicate the bias of the managers who produced them.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: CV screening algorithms must be tested for disparate impact across gender, ethnicity, age, and disability before deployment, and retested regularly. Career gaps should be treated as neutral or contextualised, not penalised. Gendered terms should be identified and neutralised during preprocessing. Training labels based on subjective human ratings should be audited for demographic bias before use.

Warning for Users: An algorithm trained to find "people like our current top performers" will replicate whatever biases exist in how those performers were selected and evaluated. If your top performers are 78% male because of historical hiring patterns, the algorithm will learn that being male is a success factor, not because it is, but because the data makes it look that way.
fields.description: How a CV Screening Algorithm Downranked Women by Penalising Career Gaps and Women's Sports

fields.title: The Anonymous Crowd That Wasn't
fields.failure_type: IoT Sensor Network / Anonymised Location Analytics
fields.deployment_context:
In 2021, a city council in northern England installed a network of Bluetooth and Wi-Fi sensors across its town centre to measure pedestrian footfall. The stated purpose was urban planning: understanding which streets were busiest, when peak hours occurred, and how events affected visitor numbers.

The council assured residents that the system was "fully anonymised." Each device (smartphone, tablet, smartwatch) was detected by its MAC address, which was immediately hashed using a one-way cryptographic function. The council published a privacy impact assessment stating that "no individual can be identified from the data collected."

The system recorded approximately 2.3 million device detections per month across 45 sensors. The data was shared with the council's planning department, local business improvement district, and a university research partner.
fields.intended_use:
In 2023, a privacy researcher at the university partner demonstrated that the "anonymised" data could be used to re-identify specific individuals with high accuracy. The technique was straightforward: because each device's hashed MAC address was consistent across all sensors, the system recorded a unique movement trail for each device.

A person who walked from their home street to the train station every morning at 7:45, visited a specific coffee shop, and returned home at 6:15 pm created a distinctive spatiotemporal pattern. The researcher showed that by combining the movement data with publicly available information such as social media check-ins, business review timestamps, and residential address data, they could match anonymised device trails to named individuals.

The researcher successfully re-identified 87 individuals from a sample of 1,000 device trails, using only publicly available information and no hacking or special access. For 23 of those individuals, the researcher could reconstruct a detailed daily routine: where they worked, which shops they visited, which pub they went to on Friday evenings, and what time they typically arrived home.

The council suspended the data-sharing agreements and commissioned an independent privacy review.

Detection: A university privacy researcher proactively tested the re-identification risk as part of a research project.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. Pseudonymisation is Not Anonymisation

Hashing a MAC address replaces a readable identifier with a scrambled one, but it's still a unique, consistent identifier. The same device produces the same hash every time, across every sensor. This is pseudonymisation (replacing a name with a code) not anonymisation (removing the ability to identify). The distinction is critical in data protection law (GDPR) and was misunderstood by the council's privacy assessment.

2. Spatiotemporal Uniqueness

Research has consistently shown that human movement patterns are highly unique. A study published in Nature found that just four spatiotemporal data points (place + time) are enough to uniquely identify 95% of individuals in a dataset. The council's sensor network collected dozens of data points per person per day which is far more than needed for re-identification.

3. Auxiliary Data Enables Linkage

The hashed data alone might be hard to link to a name. But combined with publicly available data, social media posts geotagged at specific locations, Google reviews timestamped at specific businesses, residential address databases, the movement patterns become identifiable. The council's privacy assessment considered the sensor data in isolation, without modelling the re-identification risk from combining it with other datasets.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Anonymisation must be evaluated in relation to re-identification danger, rather than only the lack of names.
