Any dataset with unique, consistent identities and spatiotemporal data could be re-identified. Privacy effect assessments should not only look at the data on its own, but also think about what someone with access to public data could learn from it. Differential privacy, temporal aggregation, and random noise injection are some of the methods that can greatly lower the chance of re-identification.

Warning for Users: "Anonymised" does not always mean private. If a system tracks your device consistently across locations and times, it creates a movement fingerprint that may be as unique as your name. When a council or company says your data is anonymous, ask: anonymous to whom, and under what assumptions?
fields.description: How a Smart City Footfall Tracker Re-Identified Individuals Despite 'Anonymised' Data

fields.title: The Children Who Didn't Fit the Pattern
fields.deployment_context:
In 2022, a multi-academy trust in the English Midlands tried out a facial recognition attendance system in three secondary schools. Cameras at the doors of schools took pictures of pupils' faces as they came in, which automatically marked them as present. The technology took the place of manual registration, which saved about 15 minutes of teaching time every day.

The seller also advertised a new function called "behavioural analytics," which would alert students whose movement patterns, facial expressions, or arrival times were very different from what was normal for them. It was said that the system was a tool for "early intervention" because it could find pupils who were having trouble before teachers could.

The academy trust's head of safety gave the system the green light because it will assist find at-risk students sooner. Parents were told in a mail that the school was "upgrading its attendance system using biometric technology."
fields.intended_use:
The behavioural analytics feature has flagged 847 "anomalous behaviour" instances in three months. The school's SENCO (Special Educational Needs Coordinator) did a study and found a worrying pattern: children with autism spectrum problems, ADHD, anxiety disorders, and Tourette's syndrome were reported 4.7 times more often than neurotypical students.

The algorithm detected actions like avoiding eye contact with the camera, taking strange paths across the building, coming at different times, making repetitive movements near sensors, and showing facial expressions that the model called "distressed" or "evasive."

For autistic pupils, many of these "anomalous" behaviours were just how they normally got around the school. One student was penalised 23 times in one month for "evasive gaze." They were autistic and naturally avoided looking someone in the eye. Before the SENCO became involved, the kids' parents were invited in for a meeting regarding "worrying behaviour patterns."

Some parents said their kids got worried about being observed and stopped going to school. One student's attendance went down from 94% to 67%. The method that was supposed to help attendance was really hurting it.

Detection: The school's SENCO found the unfair flagging trend when going over safeguarding warnings as part of her normal job.
fields.what_went_wrong:
1. 'Normal' Defined by Neurotypical Behaviour

The baseline for behaviour was set by looking at how all the pupils acted together. Because most of the students were neurotypical, the model learnt that neurotypical eye contact, movement patterns, and facial expressions were "normal." Any deviation, which is how neurodivergent students act every day, was seen as strange. The system saw neurodivergence as a sign of trouble.

2. Facial Expression Misclassification

The model's emotion recognition part learned from datasets that called direct eye contact "engaged" and looking away "evasive" or "distressed." These designations are based on neurotypical social conventions, not universal emotional states. An autistic pupil who looks away is not trying to avoid you; they may be listening better. The paradigm forced neurotypical emotional judgements on behaviour that was not typical.

3. Inadequate Consent and Proportionality

Parents were told about "biometric attendance," but they weren't told about behavioural analytics, emotion detection, or how to flag unusual behaviour. The authorisation was for tracking attendance, which is a simple and fair use. The behavioural analytics layer was a surveillance tool that had a big impact on children's rights. It was used without particular informed consent or a proportionality evaluation.
fields.recommendations:
Practical Advice: Helpful Tips: Schools and other places where kids are present should not use behavioural analytics and emotion recognition systems until they have been thoroughly tested to see how they affect neurodivergent, disabled, and minority students. Culturally and neurologically, "normal" behaviour is different, and systems that set a restricted baseline will always make differences seem like problems. If these systems are employed at all, SEND experts need to help develop them and make sure they don't have an unfair effect.

Warning for Users: A system that keeps an eye on kids and reports those who act differently is not a way to keep them safe; it is a way to make sure they follow the rules. Kids should be able to be different without being watched, marked, or labelled as sick. When a school says it's "upgrading attendance," enquire what the technology does, what data it collects, and who judges what is typical.
fields.description: How a School Attendance System Using Facial Recognition Flagged Neurodivergent Children as 'Suspicious'
